title: Siege of Jerusalem (1099)
sentences: The siege of Jerusalem from 7 June 1099 to 15 July 1099 marked the successful end of the First Crusade, and the founding of the Kingdom of Jerusalem soon afterwards.
The siege was carried out by the Christian forces of Western Europe mobilized by Pope Urban II after the Council of Clermont in 1095.
The city had been out of Christian control since the Muslim conquest of the Levant in 637 and had been held for a century first by the Seljuk Turks and later by the Egyptian Fatimids.
After an initial unsuccessful attack on 13 June, the crusaders constructed several siege engines including a siege tower and a battering ram enable them to enter the city on 15 July 1099.
Following the siege thousands of Muslims and Jews were massacred by the Crusaders.
In 1095, Pope Urban II called for a crusade at the Council of Clermont (Deos lo vult).
In addition to aiding Byzantium, which was under threat from the Seljuks, the goal was to reach the Holy Land and liberate Jerusalem.
Following their departure from Constantinople in April 1097 and their crossing of the Taurus Mountains, the main forces of the First Crusade reached northern Syria in the fall of 1097.
While Baldwin of Boulogne marched eastward and, in the spring of 1098, founded the first Crusader state, the County of Edessa, the main army laid siege at Antioch in October 1097.
After the city fell in June 1098 and the subsequent victory over a Seljuk relief army led by Kerbogha, the advance came to a standstill.
Months of political power struggles among the leaders between Bohemond of Taranto and Raymond IV of Toulouse, as well as epidemics and supply shortages, delayed the advance.
Upon taking command Raymond of Toulouse resumed the march southward in January 1099.
Following the Levantine coastline, the troops avoided protracted sieges of heavily fortified cities.
Instead, they concluded agreements with local Muslim rulers, or paid tribute.
At the end of May 1099, the army left the coastal region at Jaffa and reached the vicinity of Jerusalem on 7 June, 1099.
Since the 10th century Jerusalem had been under Fatimid rule.

The defences of the city dated back to the time of Emperor Hadrian and had been maintained and reinforced since then.The stone walls around the city stretching four kilometers long, were three meters thick and 15 meters high.

There were five major gates each guarded by a pair of towers.The city was protected on three sides by steep valleys and gorges: to the east by the Kidron Valley, to the southeast by the Hinnom Valley, and to the west by the Tyropeon Valley.
Only the southwest, over Mount Zion and along the entire length of the northern wall, offered terrain favorable for an attack.
Upon learning that a Christian army was marching to Jerusalem Iftikhar ad-Dawla the Wālī (Governor) of the city began making preparations to defend the city.
He made sure that no resources, whether water, food or wood were available for his enemies in the vicinity of the city.

He also expelled Syrian Christians who might be sympathetic to the crusading army, whereas all Jewish were permitted to stay.Anticipating that the crusaders would built siege engines, he ordered all available timber and rope to be used for build more mangonels for the city.
In the event that the Crusader machines proved capable of damaging the stone walls Iftikhar ordered to sew bags filled with straw to be placed at strategic points beside the walls.
These bags could be lowered on ropes to buffer the impact of flying rocks.
From the estimated 20,000 to 75,000 troops that have assembled at Nicaea between 12,000 and 14,000 had reached Jerusalem on 7 June.
The cavalry consisted of 1,200–1,300 men.The garrison defending Jerusalem comprised roughly some thousand Arab and Sudanese troops as well as some 400 egyptian elite cavalry.
With most wells and cisterns rendered unusable, the crusaders faced a lack of water supply.
The conditions were further exacerbated by heat, lack of shade and the khamsin.
There was only source of water, was the En-Gihon, spring that flowed from the southeast spur of the city.
It lay below the ridge that held the very first human settlements in the area, known in ancient times as Zion.
Although Gihon could deliever over a million litres a day during the winter month in summer the overall flow dropped considerably.
In opposite, the people of Jerusalem obtained all the water from deep cisterns.
In addition, there were hundreds of smaller cisterns located under houses and courtyards across the city, which were fed by a system of pipes and channels from flat roofs and paved streets.
Since the Crusaders had insufficient forces to besiege the entire city, they concentrated their strength on the sectors where they could approach the walls.
Robert of Normandy posted his troops along the northern wall, opposite the Gate of Flowers (also known as Herod's Gate).
Robert of Flanders was stationed on his right, facing the Gate of the Column (also known as St Stephen's Gate or the Damascus Gate).
Godfrey of Lorraine covered the north-west corner of the city, extending down to the Jaffa Gate.
Tancred joined him here, riding up when the army was already in position and bringing flocks he had acquired on his way from Bethlehem.
Raymond of Toulouse stood to the south.
Finding that the valley kept him too far from the walls, he moved up to Mount Zion after two or three days.
The eastern and south-eastern sectors were left unguarded.
According to Raymond of Aguilers the first attack was initiated by a prophecy of an old hermit claiming that if the crusaders would attack on 13 June until the ninth hour, it would fall to them.

During the night, the army prepared to attack the city using whatever materials they could find.Despite initial success the attack proved to be a failure, demonstrating the need for more siege engines.
Two days after the failed attack on Jerusalem on June 13, 1099, the leaders of the crusade met to discuss their strategy.
Recognizing that divine intervention would not yield the city, they were confronted by the harsh realities acknowledging that the situation, favoured the defenders of Jerusalem.
